official.title: Postdoc in Hydrodynamics, Sediment Transport and Morphological Recovery of Sand Extraction Pits
official.description_text:
Join an interdisciplinary team and use unique North Sea field observations to uncover how waves, currents, and sediment transport drive the recovery of offshore sand extraction pits.
Job description
The BACI Sand Extraction project is a multidisciplinary research programme that aims to understand the ecological, hydrodynamic, and morphodynamic impacts of offshore sand extraction. Using a Before-After-Control-Impact (BACI) approach, the project aims to unravel the processes driving the physical and ecological recovery of a medium-depth sand extraction pit over timescales ranging from individual storms to multiple years.
As part of the project, an intensive field experiment is currently taking place at a newly created 6 m deep sand extraction pit in the Dutch North Sea, and will be repeated at a later stage. Instrumented measurement frames have been installed in and around the extraction pit to monitor waves, turbulence levels, current profiles, suspended sediment concentrations, and seabed evolution during approximately one year following the extraction. These measurements are complemented by several sediment and ecological sampling campaigns and can be compared with a similar dataset acquired prior to sand extraction. Together, these observations provide a unique opportunity to analyze the physical processes controlling sediment transport and morphological adaptation following medium-depth sand extraction, while also providing the physical boundary conditions required to interpret ecological recolonization within the extraction pit. A major knowledge gap concerns how the interaction between waves, currents, turbulence, and evolving pit geometry controls sediment transport and ultimately determines the morphological recovery. In particular, it remains unclear whether recovery is dominated by rare high-energy storm events or by more progressive in filling, and how these processes vary through time as the pit evolves. Addressing these questions is essential for predicting the long-term impacts of offshore sand extraction and supporting nature-inclusive management of the North Sea.
The postdoctoral researcher will take the lead on the analysis of the hydrodynamic and morphodynamic measurements collected by the instrumented frames. An important part of the work will be to quantify how the sand extraction pit modifies waves, currents, and sediment transport processes, and to determine the mechanisms and timescales governing morphological recovery. Depending on the candidate's expertise and interests, the work may also include the application of numerical models to support the interpretation of field observations, or could include the development of innovative data-driven approaches to improve predictive capabilities. The postdoctoral researcher will furthermore closely interact with the ecological work package to establish the physical boundary conditions underpinning ecological recovery, with opportunities for a more active role in the integration of physical and ecological analyses if that fits the candidate’s interests.
The postdoctoral researcher will be based at TU Delft, working closely with Dr. Bram van Prooijen and Dr. Marion Tissier, while being embedded in a multidisciplinary research consortium involving several leading Dutch governmental, academic, and applied research institutions, including Rijkswaterstaat, Wageningen Marine Research, NIOZ, and Deltares.
This postdoctoral position is for a period of three years. The anticipated starting date is February/March 2027.
Job requirements
PhD in Hydraulic Engineering, Physical Oceanography, Physical Geography, Marine Science, or a closely related field.
Demonstrated experience in the analysis and interpretation of hydrodynamic and/or morphodynamic field or lab measurements, preferably in coastal or offshore environments.
Strong quantitative skills, including scientific programming and advanced data analysis techniques.
Enthusiasm for interdisciplinary research and willingness to collaborate with researchers from physical and ecological disciplines.

Faculty of Civil Engineering and Geosciences
The Faculty of Civil Engineering & Geosciences (CEG) is committed to outstanding international research and education in the field of civil engineering, applied earth sciences, traffic and transport, water technology, and delta technology. Our research feeds into our educational programmes and covers societal challenges such as climate change, energy transition, resource availability, urbanisation and clean water. Our research projects are conducted in close cooperation with a wide range of research institutions. CEG is convinced of the importance of open science and supports its scientists in integrating open science in their research practice. The Faculty of CEG comprises 28 research groups in the following seven departments: Materials Mechanics Management & Design, Engineering Structures, Geoscience and Engineering, Geoscience and Remote Sensing, Transport & Planning, Hydraulic Engineering and Water Management.

ai.summary: Three-year postdoctoral position in coastal hydrodynamics and morphodynamics, focused on analysing field measurements from a sand extraction pit in the Dutch North Sea. The role combines data analysis of waves, currents, and sediment transport with potential numerical modelling and integration of physical-ecological findings.

thematic_fit.rationale: The position is rooted in physical oceanography, coastal engineering, and marine geomorphology. The researcher's expertise is in human-centred XR, immersive learning, and spatial cognition. While both involve spatial reasoning, the domains are unrelated: one studies physical processes in marine systems; the other designs collaborative digital environments for human learning. No thematic overlap.

methodological_fit.rationale: Researcher has quantitative research and experimental design skills at intermediate level, which are broadly applicable. However, the core required methodologies—hydrodynamic data analysis, sediment transport physics, coastal field measurements, advanced numerical modelling (CFD), and spatial statistics on sediment patterns—are specialized to physical oceanography and absent from the researcher's profile.

growth_value.rationale: This postdoc would develop capabilities in marine physics and coastal engineering, moving away from the target identity of human-centred XR researcher. No growth pathway toward spatial learning, collaborative immersive systems, or HCI.

strategic_value.rationale: TU Delft is a priority institution. The consortium (Rijkswaterstaat, Wageningen Marine Research, NIOZ, Deltares) represents strong governmental, academic, and applied research partnerships. Supervisors (Dr. Bram van Prooijen, Dr. Marion Tissier) lead recognized groups. Three-year funding is stable. Geographic location (Netherlands, preferred region) is aligned. However, research-domain misalignment substantially reduces overall value.

eligibility_flags: Requires PhD in Hydraulic Engineering, Physical Oceanography, Physical Geography, Marine Science, or closely related field (essential). Researcher holds MSc by Research in Creative Multimedia—no evidence of coursework or thesis in coastal/marine science.

Requires demonstrated experience in analysis and interpretation of hydrodynamic and/or morphodynamic field or lab measurements, preferably coastal/offshore. Researcher's field experience is limited to user studies; no evidence of environmental monitoring, field instrumentation, or coastal data collection.

Requires strong quantitative skills including scientific programming and advanced data analysis. Researcher has intermediate quantitative-research and beginner Python—likely insufficient for the specialized data processing (hydrodynamic analysis, sediment transport algorithms, CFD interpretation) expected in this role.

Requires enthusiasm for interdisciplinary research and collaboration across physical and ecological disciplines. Researcher's interdisciplinarity is within HCI/design/XR; collaboration with marine ecologists is outside demonstrated scope.
risks: Disciplinary barrier: researcher is an HCI/design specialist; position requires marine physics expertise. No educational bridge visible.
Field measurement experience gap: researcher's lab work is user-focused; this position requires analysis of oceanographic instrumentation data (ADCPs, pressure sensors, sediment traps, etc.).
Quantitative/modelling gap: position expects proficiency in numerical modelling (CFD, advanced data-driven approaches). Researcher's quantitative toolkit is social-science oriented.
Python skill is listed as beginner with no substantial project experience. Expected to apply advanced scientific Python for hydrodynamic data processing.
High risk of mismatch during onboarding; supervisors would likely expect marine science background.

eligibility_reasons: whether a completed degree is required before employment is not stated; your MSc is still in progress — verify with the source
